There are 1000 such selections. The argument partitions the grid into 2×2 blocks.

**Setup.** Partition the 19×19 grid into a 10×10 array of blocks. Block (i,j) covers rows 2i−1, 2i and columns 2j−1, 2j, and the last block row and column are only 1 cell wide. Each block holds at most one selected cell, so 99 selected cells means exactly one block (p,q) is empty and the other 99 each hold one cell.

Describe the cell in block (i,j) by offsets (a,b) in {0,1}², where a is the row offset and b the column offset. In the last block row a is forced to 0, and in the last block column b is forced to 0.

**Forced positions.**
- In a fully occupied block row, two neighbouring blocks with b=1 then b=0 would give adjacent columns and rows differing by at most 1, which is forbidden. So b can never drop from 1 to 0 going right. Since the last block has b=0, every b in that row is 0.
- By the same argument, every a in a fully occupied block column is 0.
- Hence every block with i≠p and j≠q has offset (0,0).

**Freedom around the empty block.**
- In block row p, the blocks to the right of q must all have b=0. The blocks to the left of q can have b=1 on a suffix of blocks 1..q−1 (a suffix could be empty). This gives q choices.
- In block column q, the blocks below p must all have a=0. The blocks above p can have a=1 on a suffix of blocks 1..p−1. This gives p choices.

**One interaction.** The cell in block (p,q−1) with b=1 conflicts diagonally with the cell in block (p−1,q) with a=1. No other pair of choices conflicts.

The number of conflicting pairs is (q−1)(p−1), so the number of valid configurations for a given empty block is

pq − (p−1)(q−1) = p + q − 1.

**Sum over empty blocks.**

Σ_{p,q=1}^{10} (p+q−1) = 10·55 + 10·55 − 100 = 1000.

ANSWER: 1000
